title: Customer-class routing: operational notes and design tradeoffs
content:
Purpose
-----
This is an operational-first sketch of how we can implement customer-class (customer-tier) aware routing in the control plane and at the runtime edge across regions. Focus is on enforceable policies that map contracts/SLA tiers to routing decisions, quota modes, and noisy-neighbor mitigation without requiring per-customer bespoke code paths.

Status and context
------------------
- Draft notes for design review with SRE, serving runtime, and product (Hosted + Dedicated + Private).
- Motivated by two customer asks: (1) guaranteed p95 latency for enterprise tiers, (2) soft-deny behavior for over-consuming free tier customers.
- Should integrate with existing rollout mechanics (canaries, A/B, fallback variants) but be lightweight to operate.

Goals
-----
- Translate contract-level SLAs and customer-class into deterministic routing decisions.
- Provide quota enforcement with multiple enforcement modes (strict reject, token-bucket throttling, prioritized queuing).
- Detect noisy neighbors quickly and mitigate (throttle, isolate, schedule to separate pools).
- Support multi-region placement and graceful failover while honoring SLAs (preferred-region routing + cross-region fallback hierarchy).
- Expose clear telemetry and simple operational controls for customer-success and SRE.

Non-goals
---------
- Not a replacement for per-model admission control inside serving runtime (we will integrate with it).
- Not covering billing/chargeback flows (billing team will wire that using signals we expose).

Assumptions
-----------
- Every customer has a contract tier tag (free, standard, enterprise, premium) stored in customer metadata service.
- The control plane has an authoritative view of model compatibility and available capacity per region and capacity tier (burst vs reserved).
- Runtime supports routing hints (prefer-region, fallback-list, priority-level) and accepts per-request QoS attributes.

High-level design
-----------------
1) Policy layer in control plane (PL): declarative, evaluated per request at the edge.
   - Input: customer-id, contract-tier, route (API path/model), requested region, request token cost estimate.
   - Output: routing decision: {target pool id, qos class, quota-action, fallback list}.
2) Edge proxy/ingress: enforces QoS hints (priority queue, token-bucket checks). Logs decisions and emits metrics to the control plane.
3) Placement/runtime: enforces pool isolation (reserved pools, shared pools with cgroups), can preempt low-priority work within a pool when needed.
4) Telemetry & ops UI: per-customer dashboards (80 token/time-window, p50/p95 latency vs target, quota burn rate) and a lightweight console for on-call adjustments.

Policy language and primitives (sketch)
--------------------------------------
- match(customer.contract_tier == "enterprise") => route_to(pool="enterprise-reserved", qos= "guaranteed", quota_mode="metered")
- match(customer.contract_tier == "free" && usage_last_1h > 5x) => quota_mode = "soft-throttle"; notify(cs)
- match(route == "embeddings" && customer.contract_addon=="high-emb-slots") => prefer(pool_tags: ["emb-accelerated"]) 
Primitives:
- pool tags (reserved, burstable, gpu-v100, quantized-optimized)
- qos classes: guaranteed, prioritized, best-effort
- quota modes: reject, soft-throttle, metered
- fallback lists: ordered pool ids (region-aware)

Quota enforcement modes
-----------------------
- Reject: immediate 429-like behavior. Use for strict contract violations (rare).
- Soft-throttle: slow down request rate via token-bucket and enforce per-customer concurrency caps at the edge.
- Metered: allow through, but emit high-severity alerts when burn rate exceeds thresholds (enterprise customers rarely in this mode).
- Adaptive-burst: allow short bursts out of quota if downstream latency budget allows; controlled by burst tokens allocated per customer/billing cycle.

Noisy neighbor detection heuristics
----------------------------------
- Spike in token consumption relative to historical baseline (>5x over 5m) with concurrent increased queueing at pool level.
- Disproportionate queue depth contribution: single customer contributing >40% of pool queue depth for >30s.
- Latency impact correlation: p95 for other customers on pool rises >20% coincident with that customer activity.

Mitigation strategies
---------------------
- Local soft-throttle at edge for offending customer (fast, reversible).
- Migrate heavy traffic to a burst pool with documented cost uplift (notify customer and CS).
- Enforce stronger isolation: move to dedicated pool (reserved) for repeat offenders or per-contract requirement.
- Backpressure to SDKs: return hints (Retry-After, reduced model size suggestion) in responses for adaptive clients.

Multi-region behavior
---------------------
- Preference order: preferred-region (per contract) -> region-affinity (latency-based) -> cross-region fallback (lowest-cost healthy pool).
- Failover rules must preserve qos class: if enterprise request fails in preferred region, fallback to equivalent enterprise-reserved pool in other region; if none available, degrade to prioritized class with notification.
- Geo-proximity tagging: maintain region-to-region cost/latency matrix and prefer cross-region fallbacks that meet p95 budget.

Operational runbooks (incident example)
---------------------------------------
1) Symptom: enterprise p95 spikes for customer X in us-west-2.
2) Dashboard: check pool p95, queue depth, per-customer queue contribution.
3) Actions:
   - If pool-wide: scale reserved pool (if autoscale allowed) and promote burst capacity.
   - If single-customer noisy-neighbor: apply edge soft-throttle for customer X, open CS ticket, consider migration to separate pool.
   - If regional outage: flip routing to fallback pool following priority policy; notify customers with affected preferred-region.
4) Postmortem: capture root cause, whether policy mismatched contract, and adjust threshold or offer isolation.

Telemetry and SLOs to surface
----------------------------
- Per-customer: request_count, token_count, p50/p95/p99 latency, quota_burn_rate, throttle_events
- Per-pool: aggregate latency, healthy_capacity_pct, queue_depth, per-customer queue contribution
- Alerts: sustained quota_burn_rate > X for enterprise, pool healthy_capacity < 20%, noisy-neighbor detection triggers

Rollout plan (minimal safe path)
--------------------------------
- Phase 0: Simulate routing decisions in control plane (no enforcement). Emit "what-if" logs and dashboards for 2 weeks.
- Phase 1: Edge-level soft-throttle only for target cohorts (free and standard) behind a feature flag.
- Phase 2: Add prioritized queues and metered reporting for enterprise. Runbook and CS playbook in place.
- Phase 3: Full enforcement + cross-region failover policies. Expose operator controls in Console.

Open questions / tradeoffs
-------------------------
- Policy complexity vs observability: richer policy language allows fine-grained behavior but harder to reason about during incidents.
- How tightly should billing and enforcement be coupled? (loose coupling preferred — enforcement via control plane signals, billing in downstream systems)
- When to prefer migration to dedicated pools vs throttling? (cost threshold + SLA severity + customer contract)
- SDK client-side controls: how much adaptive behavior (model slimming, retry/backoff) do we require clients to implement vs server-side hints? 

Next steps
----------
- Sync w/ serving runtime to list required QoS APIs (prefer-region, qos-class, token-estimate, request-cost-hint). Owner: Arjun.
- Implement policy evaluator prototype in control plane (golang) and run as a canary verifier. Owner: Maya.
- Wire noisy-neighbor detection into observability pipeline and add alerting rules. Owner: SRE.
- Draft CS playbook and customer messaging templates (Sofia).

Notes to self
-------------
- Keep policy DSL intentionally small for MVP: 8–10 primitives max.
- Expect 2–3 iterations after first 6 months of production traffic to tune thresholds.

References and links
--------------------
- Related docs: PLATFORM-CUSTOMER-CLASS-2025 (confluence), PL-4821 (JIRA)
- Slack thread: #platform-routing (search ts around Jan 2025)
